## Methods

Mice and ethical approval
K18-hACE2 transgenic mice were (Jackson Laboratory, 034860) maintained in the Centre for Disease Modelling at the University of British Columbia (UBC). These experiments were approved by the Animal Care Committee at UBC, who is responsible for ensuring that all UBC animal researchers conform to the mandatory guidelines of the Canadian Council on Animal Care. The mice challenged with SARS-CoV-2 were maintained at the Toronto High Containment Facility level 3 (THCF) at the University of Toronto. These experiments were approved by the Animal Care Committee (University of Toronto), and also maintained and euthanized under humane conditions in accordance with the guidelines of the Canadian Council on Animal Care. Mice were maintained under 12 hr light/dark cycles at 20 °C ambient temperature.

Vector synthesis and preparation of saDNA and saRNA
Fig. 1A illustrates the map of the vector system discussed in this paper, hereinafter referred to as Gemini 1.0. It is based on the T7-VEE-GFP plasmid, a generous gift from Professor Steven Dowdy, at the University of California, San Diego School of Medicine,12. The vector consists of the NSP1-4 genes from the Venezuelan equine encephalitis (VEE) virus, an origin of replication site, a bacterial promoter (26S subgenomic promoter), an Ampicillin resistance (AmpR) gene acting as a selection marker for bacterial culture, a T7 promoter to recruit T7 RNA polymerase for saRNA synthesis, and a human CMV enhancer/promoter, allowing its use as a DNA or RNA vector in humans. The CMV promoter was subsequently cloned into the T7-VEE-GFP plasmid by Synbio Technologies. For the B.1.1.529 (Omicron) Spike variant of SARS CoV-2 and B.1.617.2 (Delta) spike variant of the SARS-CoV-2 virus and eGFP sequences (see Supplementary Fig. S1–5).

The Gemini 1.0 vector was transformed into DH5α Competent E. Coli (NEB, C2987), and plated onto Luria-Bertani (LB) agar containing Ampicillin for selection; this was followed by overnight culturing in LB broth at 37 °C. Vector DNA was extracted according to the EZ10 Plasmid DNA Minipreps Kit protocol (BioBasic, BS6149). This constituted the naked saDNA version of the Gemini 1.0 platform. To prepare the naked saRNA version, the Gemini 1.0 vector underwent in vitro transcription using T7 RNA polymerase (NEB, M0251L), followed by in vitro 5’ capping and 3’ polyadenylation. Figure 1 describes the self-amplifying platform pathways and in vitro replication process for both the DNA and RNA forms.

mRNA preparation
Pseudouridine substitute LNP-encapsulated mRNAs encoding eGFP (PM-LNP-21) or LNP-B.1.617.2 (Delta) spike protein variant of the SARS-CoV-2 virus (PM-LNP-12) mRNA were purchased from Promab Biotechnologies (Richmond, CA, United States). These LNP’s were formulated by Prolab with SM-102, DSPC, cholesterol, and DMG-PEG2000 at optimal molar concentration for a high rate of encapsulation and efficient mRNA delivery.

The conventional plasmid (pDNA) was either pCMV-T7-EGFP (addgene, plasmid 133962) or pCMV-Spike (addgene, plasmid 173921).

Lipid nanoparticles (LNP) formulation of Gemini saDNA and saRNA formats
The 5 µg dose of Gemini saDNA and saRNA was selected based on a thorough review of published literature on LNP-mRNA SARS-CoV-2 vaccines. Previous studies have utilized doses ranging from 0.01 µg to 10 µg, with higher doses generally yielding better immunogenicity. However, the difference in efficacy between 2 µg and 10 µg was not statistically significant, suggesting that a dose within this range would be optimal. Additionally, the formulation required a fixed nucleic acid-to-LNP ratio of 2.5:1, which further constrained the selection of an appropriate dose, with 5 µg being the maximum feasible concentration. Moreover, animal facility guidelines imposed a strict maximum injection volume of 25 µL per mouse, limiting the total amount of vaccine that could be administered. Considering these factors, a 5 µg dose was determined to be the most appropriate for the LNP-based vaccine formulations. These constraints represent an often-underappreciated aspect of all LNP-encapsulated vaccines and immunotherapies23.

The Encapsula GEN-7036 formulation, which contains a permanently charged cationic lipid (DOTAP-based), was chosen because it does not require a confined impinging jet (CIJ) turbulent mixer like Moderna Spikevax (mRNA-1273)1,2 and Pfizer–BioNTech’s Comirnaty (BNT162b2)3, and other vaccine formulations use. Instead, it can be mixed with nucleic acids at room temperature, and be freshly prepared just prior to injection. Unlike traditional LNPs that encapsulate nucleic acids within their core, permanently cationic formulations such as GEN-7036 primarily associate the nucleic acids on the particle surface. Furthermore, in preliminary head-to-head comparisons, the Encapsula GEN-7036 formulation produced higher antibody levels than the mRNA-1273-like ionizable SM-102 lipid nanoparticle formulation of the same vaccine and dose prepared using CIJ by the CDMO (Ardena Group Ltd.) (manuscript in preparation). Thus, LNP-encapsulated forms of Gemini saDNA and saRNA were prepared by mixing 5 µg of saDNA or saRNA with 18 µL of Genesome lipid solution (DOTAP:Chol:DOPE in a 1:0.75:0.5 ratio; Encapsula NanoScience, GEN-7036) in a 1:2 volume ratio at room temperature as described by the manufacturer. LNP-encapsulated nucleic acids were kept on ice until ready for injection.

LNP-mRNA preparation
Pseudouridine substitute LNP-encapsulated mRNAs encoding eGFP (Promab Biotechnologies, PM-LNP-21) or LNP-B.1.617.2 (Delta) spike protein variant of the SARS-CoV-2 virus (Promab Biotechnologies, PM-LNP-12) mRNA. These LNP’s were formulated by Promab Biotechnologies with SM-102, DSPC, cholesterol, and DMG-PEG2000 at optimal molar concentrations for a high rate of encapsulation and efficient mRNA delivery.

HEK293 cell culture and transfection with Gemini
HEK293 cells (ATCC; CRL-1573) were cultured in Dulbecco’s Modified Eagle Medium (DMEM; Gibco, 11965-092) containing 10% Fetal Bovine Serum (FBS; Gibco, A3160702) and 1:100 dilution of penicillin/streptomycin solution (Thermo Fisher Scientific, 15140122). Cells were seeded at a density of 5×105 cells per well in a 6-well plate 1 day prior to transfection. Transfection was performed with ~2.5 µg of either Gemini saDNA or saRNA using the Lipofectamine™ 3000 protocol (Thermo Fisher Scientific, L3000001) and was carried out without drug selection to either kanamycin or puromycin resistance encoded by the Gemini 1.0 vector.

Negative (-) strand mRNA detection
HEK293 cells were harvested 72 h post-transfection. Total RNA was extracted using the PureLink™ RNA Mini Kit (Ambion, 12183025), and its integrity was checked on a 0.8% agarose gel. Molecular weight marker used was 1 Kb Plus DNA Ladder (Froggabio, DM015. Thereafter, total RNA was treated with amplification grade DNase I (Invitrogen, 18068015) to remove any residual DNA, followed by first strand cDNA synthesis using either a NSP4 gene-specific forward primer with a random nucleotide tag sequence (5’-cggtcatggtggcgaataaGCGGCCTTTAATGTGGAATG-3) or without any primer according to the SuperScript™ III Reverse Transcriptase protocol (Invitrogen, 18080044). cDNA synthesis was then completed followed by a PCR using an eGFP gene-specific reverse primer (5’-CACCTTGATGCCGTTCTTCT-3’) and the random nucleotide tag-specific forward primer (5’-cggtcatggtggcgaataa-3’) to produce a 1.9 kb band which would be an indication of negative RNA strand. A nested PCR using the forward primer, 5’-CCGAGAGCTGGTTAGGAGATTA-3’, and reverse primer, 5’-GCTTGTCGGCCATGATATAGA-3’ on the first PCR product was then performed to amplify cDNA with a band size of 1.4 kb to verify the correct target sequence (see Fig. 1C). PCRs were run on a Bio-Rad T100 Thermocycler and parameters used for both PCRs were: 94 °C for 30 s, 56 °C for 30 s, 72 °C for 30 s, for 28 cycles.

Flow cytometry sample preparation
HEK293 cells were transfected with either: a) Gemini saDNA expressing SARS-CoV-2 spike protein, or b) a non-self-amplifying DNA plasmid control expressing SARS-CoV-2 spike, or c) LNP-B.1.617.2 (Delta) spike protein variant of the SARS-CoV-2 virus mRNA, or d) the conventional LNP-encapsulated Pseudouridine substitute mRNAs encoding the B.1.617.2 (Delta) spike protein variant of the SARS-CoV-2 virus, (see Fig. 2 for method overview). Cells were harvested at 2- and 6 days post-transfection as were the FACS samples and resuspended in FACS buffer at a concentration of 1.0×106 cells/mL. Subsequently, cells were incubated in FACS buffer for 30 min at 4 °C for Fc blocking, centrifuged (240xg for 4 min at 4 °C), and then stained with an anti-receptor-binding domain (RBD) SARS-CoV-2 spike antibody conjugated to Alexa Fluor 647 (1:100; Invitrogen, 51-6490-82) for 30 min at 4 °C in the dark. Cells were then washed in FACS buffer by centrifuging at 240xg for 4 min at 4 °C) and resuspended in FACS buffer (500 uL/tube). Data was acquired using a BD Cytoflex flow cytometer.

Fluorescence-activated cell sorting (FACS) sample preparation
HEK293 cells were transfected with either: a) Gemini saDNA expressing eGFP, or b) Gemini saRNA expressing eGFP, or c) LNP-encapsulated pseudouridine-substituted mRNAs encoding eGFP (Promab Biotechnologies, PM-LNP-21). Two days post-transfection, cells were sorted for eGFP expression. Cells were then harvested at 14- and 28 days post-transfection using Cellstripper® (Corning, 25-056-CI), and counted using a TC20 Automated Cell Counter (Bio-Rad, 1450102), assessing live cells with a 1:1 dilution with 0.4% Trypan Blue (Gibco, 15250-061). Cells were then resuspended in FACS buffer (1X phosphate buffered saline (PBS) with 2% FBS and 2% normal rabbit serum) at a concentration of 1.0×106 cells/mL and incubated in FACS buffer for 30 min at 4 °C for Fc receptor blocking. Blocked cells were again centrifuged at 240xg for 4 min at 4 °C, and resuspended in FACS buffer (500 µL/tube).

Western blot
HEK293 cells were transfected with either: (a) Gemini saDNA or saRNA expressing the SARS-CoV-2 spike, or (b) Gemini saDNA or LNP-encapsulated pseudouridine-substituted mRNAs encoding eGFP (Promab Biotechnologies, PM-LNP-21), or (c) LNP-encapsulated mRNA encoding the B.1.617.2 (Delta) spike variant of SARS-CoV-2 (Promab Biotechnologies, PM-LNP-12). Cells were harvested 72 h post-transfection, lysed in 2X sample buffer supplemented with 5% β-Mercaptoethanol (BME; Bio-Rad, 1610710), and heated at 90 °C for 10 min. Subsequently, samples were treated with Benzonase nuclease (Sigma, E1014) for 3 h to remove nucleic acids. A total of 30 µg of protein per well was loaded onto a 4-15% precast SDS-PAGE gel (Bio-Rad, 4561083). SDS-PAGE gels were run on the Bio-Rad Mini-PROTEAN® Tetra Vertical Electrophoresis Cell and the running conditions were as follows: 75 V for 20 min, then 120 V for 2 h, in running buffer (100 mM Tris, 100 mM Tricine, 0.1% SDS). Molecular weight marker used was BLUelf Prestained Protein Ladder (Froggabio, PM008). For Western blot, protein was transferred to a nitrocellulose membrane using the Bio-Rad Trans-Blot® Cell at 75 V for 3 h in Towbin buffer (2.5 mM Tris, 19.2 mM glycine, 2% (v/v) methanol). Subsequently, the membrane was washed in 0.1% Tween-20 in PBS (PBST), followed by blocking with 5% skim milk in 1% PBST for 2 h. Primary antibodies for ALFA Tag (Nano-tech, N1581) and eGFP (Thermo Fisher Scientific, GFP-101AP) were diluted 1:5000 and incubated with the membrane at 4 °C overnight. The membrane was then washed three times for 10 min each with 0.1% PBST. Anti-rabbit (Thermo Fisher Scientific, 31460) and anti-mouse (Abcam, AB205719) secondary antibodies conjugated to horseradish peroxidase (HRP) were diluted 1:5000 and incubated with the membrane at room temperature for 1 h, followed by three 10 min washes of 0.1% PBST. Subsequent signal detection was conducted on a ChemiDoc MP Imaging System (Bio-Rad).

Qualitative determination of eGFP expression in injected mouse leg muscles
Two groups of nine 6–12 week-old K18-hACE2 mice were injected with 5 µg of either LNP-saRNA or LNP-saDNA expressing eGFP, by intramuscular injection into the caudal thigh muscle. For each group, mice were sacrificed, at 14, 28 or 42 days post-injection (n=3 per day of sacrifice). Three mice injected only with saline were used as background controls and sacrificed on day 2 (n=3). Thigh muscles were excised and immediately frozen on dry ice in Epredia™ Neg-50™ frozen section medium (Fisher Scientific, 36-101-4314). Samples were stored at -80 °C until sectioned using a cryostat microtome and counter-stained with DAPI at The Centre for Phenogenomics (TCP), University of Toronto. Images were captured at the TCP facility (Fig. 4) and were subsequently assessed for qualitative expression of native eGFP. For each sample, four sectioned layers per sample were assessed, and the one with highest eGFP intensity was chosen per sample. A visual average was ascertained from these images for each time point and a suitable representative image was selected (Fig. 4B).

The highest eGFP intensity images were used to quantify eGFP mean intensity (Fig. 4C, D), utilizing ImageJ software to calculate mean intensity and total area for each sample. Weighted mean intensities were calculated for each vaccine group per time point, as the sum of the individual weighted mean eGFP intensities per sample. The individual weighted means were calculated using the following equation: (area sample / total area per time point) × mean intensity sample.

Immunization of mice
Groups of 15 week-old K18-hACE2 transgenic mice (Jackson Laboratory, 034860) were immunized with 5 µg of LNP-encapsulated or 50 µg naked saDNA or saRNA formats expressing the B.1.617.2 (Delta) spike protein variant of the SARS-CoV-2 virus or eGFP, or 50 µg naked saDNA or saRNA formats expressing the B.1.1.529 (Omicron) spike variant of the SARS-CoV-2 vaccine (see Supplementary Fig. S1 for the sequence). Optimal doses were determined in prior experiments utilizing other Spike constructs (Fig. 6B, C). Mice were immunized by intramuscular injection into the right caudal thigh muscle. Blood samples were taken from the left lateral saphenous vein before vaccination at day 1, and day 28 or day 42 post-initial vaccination. During the study, mice were monitored weekly (or more frequently if needed after injections or blood collection) for any behavioural changes or changes to body condition or weight. A humane endpoint was determined as a 20% overall weight loss or 10% weight loss from previous weight.

Cytokine bead-based array
Blood from mice was collected in 500 µL serum microvette tubes (Sarstedt, 20.1343.100) and centrifuged at 2000xg for 10 min at 4 °C. Serum was transferred to a fresh 500 µL microtube. Both leg muscles were collected, cut into small pieces with scissors, then incubated in 1 mL of Pierce™ RIPA Lysis Buffer (Thermofisher, PI89900) for 20 min at 4 °C. The sheared tissue was then sonicated with titanium beads for 20 min and centrifuged at 10,000xg for 10 min at 4 °C. Supernatant was transferred to a fresh 5 mL macrotube. Serum and leg muscle supernatants were mixed with 100X Halt™ Protease and Phosphatase Inhibitor Cocktail (Thermofisher, 78443) and 100X Penicillin-Streptomycin Solution (Thermofisher, 15140122), and stored at –70 °C prior to analysis.

The BD™ Cytometric Bead Array (CBA) Mouse Th1/Th2/Th17 CBA Kit (BD Biosciences, 560485) was used to determine cytokine concentrations from the serum and leg muscle supernatants. The protocol provided in the kit was followed. Samples were run on a Beckman Coulter CytoFLEX Flow Cytometer. Data was analyzed using CBA Analysis Software (V1.1.15) and visualized using GraphPad Prism (V10.1.1).

ELISA Protocols
All ELISA assays followed the same general workflow with antigen-specific variations noted below. Coating antigens or antibodies were diluted in coating buffer (0.1 M Carbonate, pH 9.5) and coated onto 96-well plates (Corning, 3369) overnight at 4 °C. Plates were washed four times with washing buffer (0.1% Tween-20 in 1X PBS), then blocked with blocking buffer (2% BSA, 0.1% Tween-20 in 1X PBS) overnight at 4 °C, followed by five washes with washing buffer. Serum samples from immunized mice were serially diluted in blocking buffer. One hundred microliters of each dilution were added to wells and plates were incubated away from light at 37 °C for 1 h. After washing, the appropriate secondary detection antibody was added and incubated at 37 °C for 1 h. Following additional washes, 100 µL/well of TMB substrate (Thermo Fisher Scientific, 34028) was added and incubated away from light at room temperature. The reaction was stopped by adding 100 µL/well of stopping solution (0.16 N H2SO4) and absorbance was read at 450 nm using an ELISA plate reader. Background absorbance from negative control wells (containing blocking buffer without serum) was subtracted from all sample measurements prior to data analysis and visualization67. Outliers were identified using Grubbs’ test (p<0.05) and excluded from subsequent analysis.

SARS-CoV-2 Spike ELISA
For Delta strain analysis, SARS-CoV-2 Super Stable Trimer Spike protein (ACROBiosystems, SPN-C52H9-50UG) was used as the coating antigen. For Omicron strain analysis, SARS-CoV-2 RBD of spike protein (Proteogenix, Strain B.1.1.529, PX-COV-P074) was used. Serum samples were collected from mice immunized with either the B.1.617.2 (Delta) or B.1.1.529 (Omicron) spike protein variant. Standard curves were generated using GraphPad Prism (Version 10.0.1). For Delta, a B.1.617.2 SARS-CoV-2 spike antibody standard (ACROBiosystems, S1N-S58A1) was used. For Omicron, a positive control serum was generated in-house by vaccinating mice with Omicron spike protein in alum adjuvant, and quantified antibody from this serum was used to construct the standard curve. Unknown antibody values were interpolated from the respective standard curves and expressed in ng/mL. The secondary antibody used was Goat anti-mouse IgG, HRP-conjugated (Southern Biotech, 1030-05).

SARS-CoV-2 Nucleocapsid ELISA
Nucleocapsid capture antibody (Acrobiosystem, NUN-CH14) was coated at 4.7 µg/mL. Serum samples from SARS-CoV-2 virally challenged mice were diluted 3-fold from 1:240 to 1:2160. A biotinylated anti-nucleocapsid secondary capture antibody (Acrobiosystem, AM223; 1 µg/mL dilution) was applied for 1 h at 37 °C, followed by streptavidin-HRP secondary (Jackson ImmunoResearch, 016-030-084; 1:1000 dilution) for 1 h at 37 °C. TMB substrate incubation time was 10 min at room temperature. A standard curve was generated from serial 2-fold dilutions of nucleocapsid protein (Acrobiosystems, NUN-C52Hw) ranging from 3.2 ng/mL to 0.05 ng/mL using GraphPad Prism (Version 10.0.2). Unknown sample concentrations were interpolated from the standard curve and expressed in ng/mL.

eGFP ELISA
eGFP protein (Thermofisher Scientific, A42613) was coated at 100 ng/mL. Serum samples from mice immunized with eGFP protein were diluted 3-fold from 1:80 to 1:2160. The Goat anti-mouse HRP-conjugated secondary antibody (Thermo Fisher Scientific, 31430; 1:4000 dilution) was applied for 1 h at 37 °C. TMB substrate incubation time was 20 min at room temperature. An anti-GFP antibody standard (Thermo Fisher Scientific, GFP-101AP) was used to generate the standard curve using GraphPad Prism (Version 9.4.1). Unknown antibody values were interpolated from the standard curve and expressed in ng/mL.

ELISPOT assay protocols
Pre-coated ELISPOT plates were washed with PBS and seeded with spleen cell suspensions (3–5×10⁵ cells/well) in complete medium (RPMI with 10% FBS), with an initial incubation period of 30 min at room temperature for plate blocking. Following overnight rest, lipopolysaccharide (2 µg/mL) and dendritic cells (DC 2.4; 1:10 ratio, 3–5×10⁴ cells/well) were added as antigen-presenting cells. SARS-CoV-2 overlapping spike peptides (JPT Peptide Technologies GmbH, PepMix™; 1 µg/mL) were added for antigen-specific T cell stimulation, optimizing epitope coverage along the protein sequence. Plates were incubated in a humidified chamber at 37 °C with 5% CO₂ for the assay-specific duration. After incubation, plates were washed with PBS, incubated with biotinylated secondary antibody, followed by Streptavidin-HRP, and developed with substrate. Spots were read using an ELISPOT reader system (Autoimmun Diagnostika GmbH, ELR02) and analyzed using GraphPad Prism. Background values were subtracted from all sample measurements prior to data analysis and visualization67. Outliers were identified using Grubbs’ test (p<0.05) and excluded from subsequent analysis.

Interferon-γ ELISPOT. Pre-coated ELISPOT plates (Mabtech, 3321-4HST-2) were blocked with 200 µL of complete medium (RPMI with 20% or 10% FBS). Following overnight cell rest and addition of LPS and dendritic cells, peptides from the SARS-CoV-2 Omicron variant (B.1.1.529) spike protein were added. Plates were incubated for 48 h. Biotinylated secondary antibody (Mabtech, 3321-6) and Streptavidin-HRP (Mabtech, 3310-9) were applied, followed by TMB substrate for spot development.

TNF-α ELISPOT. Pre-coated ELISPOT plates (Immunospot, mTNFap-2M/2) were used without blocking buffer. Following overnight cell rest and addition of LPS and dendritic cells, SARS-CoV-2 spike peptides were added. Plates were incubated for 24 h. Biotinylated secondary antibody and Streptavidin-HRP (both Immunospot, mTNFap-2M/2) were applied, followed by Immunospot Blue Developer solution for spot development.

IL-4 ELISPOT. Pre-coated ELISPOT plates (Immunospot, mIL4p-2M/2) were used without blocking buffer. Following overnight cell rest and addition of LPS and dendritic cells, SARS-CoV-2 spike peptides were added. Plates were incubated for 24 h. Biotinylated secondary antibody and Streptavidin-HRP (both Immunospot, mIL4p-2M/2) were applied, followed by Immunospot Blue Developer solution for spot development.

Measuring viraemia in virally challenged mice
K18-hACE2 transgenic mice were purchased from the Jackson Laboratory and maintained in the Division of Comparative Medicine CL3, Viral Core & Biobank at the University of Toronto. These experiments were approved by the Animal Care Committee (University of Toronto). Animals were maintained and euthanized under humane conditions in accordance with the guidelines of the Canadian Council on Animal Care. In separate experiments, 3 male and 3 female 6–12 week-old K18-hACE2 transgenic mice were used to evaluate viral load in mice vaccinated with 5 µg of LNP-encapsulated Delta (B.1.617.2) spike protein, LNP-encapsulated or naked Omicron (B.1.1.529) spike protein encoded by saDNA, or PBS controls. A second vaccine dose of 5 µg was given 28 days following the initial dose (of 5 µg; both injected intramuscularly) after which virus challenge was presented 14 days later (on Day 42). The LNP-encapsulated Delta (B.1.617.2) spike protein group was challenged with the Delta (B.1.617.2) strain of coronavirus variants administered nasally. While the LNP-encapsulated Omicron (B.1.1.529) spike protein encoded by saDNA or naked saDNA was challenged with the Omicron (B.1.1.529) strain of the SARS CoV-2 coronavirus variant administered nasally. All mice in the Delta (B.1.617.2) strain of coronavirus group were challenged with 1.6×105 viral units/dose of the Delta (B.1.617.2) SARS-CoV-2 virus. The second group consisted of mice vaccinated with saDNA containing the Omicron (B.1.1.529) Spike protein and from mice given no vaccine (i.e., saline only). The mice in this group were vaccinated with the 5 µg of vaccine and on the same schedule as were the mice in the first group. All mice in this group were challenged with 1.0×105 viral units/dose of the Omicron (B.1.1.529) SARS-CoV-2 virus. Serum was collected by cardiac puncture and stored at -20 °C prior to testing.

SARS-CoV-2 pseudotyped virus neutralization assay with GFP reporter
Preparation of SARS-CoV-2 Omicron pseudotyped virus. To generate working batches of SARS-CoV-2 Omicron pseudo-typed virus, HEK293T cells (70%-80% confluent) were transfected with the plasmid pcDNA3.3_SARS2_omicron_BA.1 (Addgene, 180375) using the Lipofectamine 3000 transfection reagent. Approximately 24 h after transfection, cells were infected with the G*ΔG-VSV virus, where the G gene is replaced with the GFP reporter at a multiplicity (MOI) of ~3 to 5. To regenerate working stocks of G*ΔG-VSV virus, cells were transfected with pCAGGS-G and infected with G*ΔG-VSV at low MOI of 0.1 instead. One-hour post-infection, the cell supernatant was removed and the cells were washed with 1X PBS at least three times before replenishing the media with complete culture medium. The first batch of supernatant was collected 24 h after infection and can be stored at 2–8 °C. The cells were then replenished with complete media for another 24 h, after which the supernatant can be collected again. The collected pseudo-typed virus harvests were combined, spun, and filtered through a 0.45 µm filter. One microgram of anti-VSV-G antibody was added to the SARS-CoV-2 Omicron pseudo-typed virus stock and aliquoted into 1 mL cryovials for storage at -80 °C.

Antibody neutralization assay with SARS-CoV-2 Omicron pseudo typed virus. In a clear, 96-well flat-bottom culture plate (Falcon, 08-772-2C), the outermost wells were filled with 200 µL of sterile PBS or water to avoid edged drying effects. Serum sample dilutions were prepared by initially diluting 1:20, followed by two serial 5-fold dilutions. The positive control, anti-SARS-CoV-2 RBD neutralizing antibody (S2K146; ProteoGenix, PTXCOV-A582), was used to create a standard log curve for quantifying antibody titers. The positive antibody had an initial dilution of 1:1000 with serial 3-fold dilutions performed in duplicates. 50 µL of the SARS-CoV-2 Omicron pseudotyped virus stock was mixed with 10 µL of the diluted samples in duplicates. Cell control wells had no serum or virus, while the virus control wells had no serum. The plate was placed in a 37 °C incubator for at least 1 h. After incubation, VERO cells were prepared and adjusted to a cell concentration of 2-3×105 cells/mL with complete DMEM medium. 100 µL of the cell suspension was added to all 60 inner wells, and the plate was incubated in the 37 °C cell culture incubator for 20–28 h. After incubation, the plates were spun at 600xg for 5 min to bring the cells to the bottom of the wells. The cells were then fixed with 4% PFA pH 7.4 and stained with 300 nM DAPI. The plates could be stored at 2–8 °C however it is recommended to measure the plate as soon as possible since the fluorescence will diminish over time even when fixed. To assess and quantify cells exhibiting fluorescence, the CellInsight CX5 High Content Screening (HSC) instrument (Thermo Fisher Scientific) was used to read the neutralization assay plates. Software assay parameters were set to measure GFP and DAPI fluorescence in the cells. Positive GFP cells were only considered if they overlapped with DAPI-positive cells to differentiate them from cellular debris. The raw dataset was exported as an Excel spreadsheet.

To calculate the concentration of neutralizing antibodies in the serum or tested samples, the exported raw data was first used to calculate percent neutralization and then interpolated against the standard curve generated. Percentage neutralization was calculated as follows: (1.0-[percent of GFP from samples/percent of GFP from virus control samples]) x 100. A standard log scale was generated by plotting the log of antibody concentrations against the readout measurements. The concentration of neutralizing antibodies in the samples was then interpolated from the log standard curve which was generated from the known concentrations of antibody S2K146.

Estimation of frequency of genomic integration
Within the Supplementary information, the Supplementary Method for determining the frequency of genomic integration, along with corresponding references is included. The methods and results are further explained in Supplementary Fig. S6 and 7, and Supplementary Tables S1 and S2.

Statistical analysis
Vaccine data was first analysed for significant outliers in GraphPad Prism (Version 9.4.1 or 10.0.0) using Grubbe’s test. This data was then analysed using the Psych package in RStudio (R version 4.2.0). The resulting summary statistics were used to assess skewness and kurtosis of data distribution. Shapiro-Wilk and Kolmogorov-Smirnoff tests were performed in R to measure the parameters of normal distributions. Normally distributed data was subjected to Student’s t-test (for two groups) where error bars represented standard deviation (SD), or Analysis of Variance (ANOVA) statistical test (both using the GraphPad Prism software, version 9.4.1 or 10.0.0) along with Tukey’s and Dunnett’s post-hoc tests to test the differences between more than two groups. Each point on the Figure denotes individual animal in the experiment. p-values <0.05 were considered significant using 95% confidence intervals.

## Round 1 — Reviewer Comments

### Reviewer 1

Jefferies et al. claimed the development of a binary self-amplifying nucleic acid platform that could eliminate the requirement of vectors in vaccine applications. However, many design of their experiments were poor and evidences/data did not support their claims. It looks like they are over-selling their platform. It is not recommend for publication in this high-quality journal.
Major issues:
1. SaRNAs have long been developed and proposed as a vaccine platform. Their corresponding plasmid (i.e., saDNA) were also designed and used for IVT production of saRNA. We did not see a unique design of self-amplifying nucleic acid platform was developed such as using an improved replicon to facilitate the elimination of lipid nanoparticles and the mechanism was disclosed (why this design could enable the elimination of vectors). It seems that there is no improvement in design compared to reported ones (10.1016/j.ymthe.2017.11.017; 10.1038/s41467-020-17409-9; 10.1016/j.ymthe.2021.04.001.).
2. Experiments were poorly designed. The authors should compare LNP-saDNA, LNP-saRNA, saDNA, saRNA and LNP-mRNA throughout their studies if they intended to demonstrated the superiority of their self-amplifying nucleic acid platform. However, many studies were lack of experimental groups. Moreover, the authors used different LNPs (DOTAP) when comparing their vaccines with LNP-mRNA (SM-102). Further, the author used different doses for different vaccines, which made their comparison unfair. In some animal studies, the authors vaccinated mice once, while in others, the authors vaccinated mice twice, which made it more difficult to compare the efficacy.
3. The in vitro/vivo expression kinetics of LNP-saDNA, LNP-saRNA, saDNA, saRNA and LNP-mRNA should be thoroughly studied over a longer period. The time point of expression peak should be reflected. For in vivo expression, luciferase is recommended as a reporter gene to enable consecutive, long-term observation (> 1 month).
4. DNA and AAV should be used and compared to Gemini-D in order to support their claim about lower genetic integration.
5. A major concern of saDNA and saRNA is toxicity. The reactogenicity/inflammation (e.g., serum TNF-alpha, IP-10 and MCP-1) should be studied in vivo and compared with mRNA-LNP.
6. It is not fair to compare the integrity of saDNA, saRNA with mRNA-LNP after repeated freezing and thawing. SaDNA and saRNA are molecules, while mRNA-LNP is a complex. Also, mRNA-LNP is not designed for repeated freezing and thawing. Instead, the thermostability/integrity of cargoes should be compared between saDNA, saRNA and mRNA-LNP.
7. IgG data from mice should not be compared to human IgG data. Could the authors give examples where IgM is important for vaccine development?
8. GFP was used as antigen. Please justify it. It is recommended that Spike is used as antigen to keep consistent.
Minor issues
9. The Introduction (especially at the beginning) is too broad and deviated from scope of the work.
10. Page 47, line 5, it should be LNP-encapsulated mRNA.
11. Figure 4D and 8A, there are too limited replicates/mice in each group (n = 2). In many graphs (Figures 5, 8), each data point should be shown.
12. Figure 4c, a scheme is needed to show the workflow of this experiment.
13. Figure 5, The GFP signals in DNA and RNA seem stronger than saDNA and saRNA.
14. Page 10, line 10. Figure 5D is wrong.
15. Some sentences are repetitive. Page 12, line 1, this sentence can be combine with the last one. And Page 18, line 9.

### Reviewer 3

The manuscript by Jefferies et al details the creation of lipid nanoparticle free self-amplifying nucleic acid vaccine platforms, with reported benefits over conventional nanomedicines that if true could provide significant advancements for this type of therapy/vaccine platforms. The authors claim to benchmark their platforms against conventional mRNA, but there are limited head-to-head comparison or studies not designed appropriately to enable direct comparison. While the authors demonstrate freeze-thaw stability and T cell and antibody responses are induced post-vaccination, claims of superiority to current mRNA LNP technologies are not supported by current data and therefore precludes publication of the manuscript at this point in time.
Major comments:
Comparison studies not performed at the same time: Data in figure 3 and figure 4 appears to be derived from independent experiments (based on differences in background population in flow plots and gates). It feels as though the LNP mRNA was included as a request from a previous reviewer, and is there to highlight difference in length of antigen expression, which is important data to show. But if the authors are including this data, then they must clearly state data was acquired in independent experiments and not analyse data together in a single statistical test.
Statistical analysis primarily compare response to naïve control: if the focus of the immunology study is to show the vaccine is immunogenic, then this analysis would be appropriate, but the underlying tone of the paper is comparison of platforms, therefore the statistical analysis should be focussed on comparing vaccine groups and p values on plots indicating these differences (or lack of which there predominately is).
Immunogenicity experiments performed with different doses of vaccine: Figure 8 is included to demonstrate that LNP formulation isn’t required, but there is a large range in antigen dose 100ug Gemini-D, 25ug Gemini-R and 5ug LNP mRNA. Overall the data shows no difference in immunogenicity, but if the dose of antigen was normalised then LNP vaccines would show vastly superior responses. If it isn’t possible to have equivalent antigen doses between platforms, then a head to head comparison in a dose ranging study for each vaccine should be performed, this would give the reader confidence that the vaccine doses weren’t cherry picked.
Lack of direct head to head comparison: Fig 9 investigates the duration of antibody responses, and suggest naked saDNRA or saRNA “result in extended and stronger antibody responses” but compared to what, there is no comparator vaccine in this study. The claim of superiority needs to be tempered.
Fig 10 compares the efficacy of naked vs saRNA, each group is compared to naïve controls then reduction in viral load between groups compared. This analysis should all be performed in a single statistical analysis and presented in a single graph if the experiment was performed at the same time with the same naïve controls, otherwise this is not a proper head to head comparison.
Minor comments:
There is a lack of attention to detail across the paper and doesn’t give the reader confidence in the data.
Figure 5 contains images of the same magnification, but then there is differences between size bars, indicating images have been stretched or not at the same scale.
Figure 8B not all data points are displayed and the error bar is cropped from the top of the graph.
Figure 8A IgM contains only 2 data points but was an experiment of 4 (?) mice.
Unvaccinated control data is not shown, yet this is the focus of the statistical analysis.
Dose and constructs shift between experiments. Figure legends lack detail on number of replicate experiments, dose of vaccine and particular vaccine construct.

### Reviewer 4

In this manuscript, the authors compare a self-amplifying nucleic acid platform (mRNA and armed DNA) with LNP-formulated nucleic acid vaccines to show that LNP formulation may be omitted to obtain good vaccine responses.
The system is based on the “Gemini” replicon-based self-amplifying dual expression vector which contains both a T7 promoter for in vitro transcription and a CMV promoter for mRNA production if delivered as DNA in cells or tissues. The authors confirm the presence of negative strand RNA synthesis after transfection of the Gemini system using a GFP expression-based Gemini approach first, followed by proof of SARS-CoV-2 Delta Spike protein production.
The vaccine platforms described are very interesting and promising, however they require more in vivo work for proper validation as I suggest below:
Is the decline in GFP expression observed in vitro after LNP-mRNA transfection due to dying cells or is this exhaustion of the mRNA pool used for transfection?
Line 4 page 11: what is blue ice? Dry ice?
In Fig 3, the Gemini system is delivered using LNP formulation to facilitate transfection. In other figures or in vivo, no LNP formulation is mentioned and I assume not used for delivery of the Gemini system. It would add to the clarity of the manuscripts if this was made more clear when LNP formulation was actually used or not.
Fig. 6: can the gel bands be quantified to provide a more quantitative measure of degradation/stability for the different vaccine types? Typo in the legend: … gel images were documents… should be …. gel images were documented…
Page 14: typo: signally needs to be signaling.
Figure 8: please show the values for the unvaccinated control groups in all panels as well. Panel B: error bar is not fully displayed, Panel C: how many mice per group?
Page 13-14: the authors suggest that different TLR signaling may be the reason for the different outcomes of the antibody response. Unmethylated DNA and RNA can also be sensed by innate immune sensors other than TLRs. It is likely that the cGAS-STING pathway will be involved in sensing as well.
I would suggest that a microneutralisation assay needs to be done with the immune sera of vaccinated mice to correlate ELISA binding titers with more functional antibodies that can neutralize virus. This will help to understand better the quality of the vaccine response.
Page 17: the values for antibody responses to saRNA should also be shown until day 84 post vaccination to allow fair comparison between the saRNA and saRNA and saDNA system. Was an LNP-formulated mRNA control included in this durability study. Again, microneutralization titers generated with these sera would be more informative than ELISA binding titers alone.
Page. 17 line 12: typo in paragraph title
The protection experiment shown in Fig. 10 raises many questions: Omicron variants show very poor replication and cause no disease in animal models. Which Omicron variant was used for challenge. Why was nucleocapsid protein in blood used as a read out for viral load? Plaque assay, TCID50 or even qPCR for subgenomic RNA would make more sense. What was the rationale for challenging mice at 5 days post booster vaccination. This is very short after vaccination, and antibody titers will still go up for many days post booster vaccination. Presence of nucleocapsid protein in blood does not perse mean blood viremia, as stated by the authors. It would have made more sense if the authors had used the Delta-based vaccines and had challenged with the Delta variant, which actually is pathogenic in K18 mice.

Highlights of the Dual-Format Innovation:
The Gemini platform is a binary system that combines the best features of self-amplifying RNA (saRNA) and self-amplifying DNA (saDNA) technologies. This dual-format approach is indeed novel and offers two distinct advantages:
Gemini-R (RNA-based): Delivers rapid antigen expression, ideal for emergency responses or acute vaccination scenarios.
Gemini-D (DNA-based): Provides exceptional stability, simplified manufacturing, and long-term storage solutions.
These complementary technologies allow for greater flexibility and adaptability, something that no other single-platform system currently offers. While saRNA platforms based on Venezuelan equine encephalitis virus (VEEV) are well studied, the application of a self-amplifying armed DNA (saDNA) framework, especially as part of a binary vaccine system, remains completely unexplored. This addresses a critical gap in the literature, emphasizing the platform’s novelty.
Manufacturing Efficiency:
The Gemini platform’s ability to eliminate the need for lipid nanoparticle (LNP) encapsulation is a direct response to some of the most challenging bottlenecks faced by current mRNA vaccines. Conventional mRNA-based vaccines are reliant on LNPs for stability and delivery, which adds complexity and cost to production. In contrast:
Gemini-D leverages a plasmid DNA-based vector that is self-amplifying, allowing for simpler, scalable manufacturing. This represents a tangible improvement in production economics and logistics, especially in resource-limited settings where LNP formulations are difficult to implement.
Our data clearly show significant reductions in adverse reactions due to the absence of LNPs, a well-known challenge in current mRNA vaccine systems.
Cost-Effectiveness and Scalability:
Critically, Gemini-D’s plasmid-based system enables low-cost, high-volume manufacturing with minimal reliance on sophisticated equipment, which can be a significant advantage for rapid global deployment. The absence of LNPs directly reduces production costs and complexity, making the platform a viable option for large-scale manufacturing under standard conditions.
Enhanced Stability and Distribution:
One of the strongest points of the Gemini platform is its enhanced stability, which the reviewer overlooks:
Gemini formulations are stable across multiple freeze/thaw cycles and can be freeze-dried, stored, and reconstituted without losing efficacy. This contrasts with current mRNA vaccines that degrade rapidly after just one freeze/thaw cycle and require ultra-cold storage (-20°C to -80°C).
The ability to store and transport Gemini formulations at ambient temperatures (2°C to 8°C) offers substantial benefits in terms of global distribution, particularly in remote or low-resource areas where maintaining cold chain logistics is a major hurdle.
Prolonged Protein Expression and Immunogenicity:
Our studies demonstrate that the Gemini platform supports prolonged protein expression for over 28 days, compared to the mere 3-day window observed with traditional mRNA vaccines. This extended expression period leads to a sustained immune response—a critical aspect of durable and effective immunization strategies. We further substantiate this with preclinical models showing that the self-amplifying DNA format elicits robust antibody responses and mitigates viraemia, which is key for reducing pathogen replication and transmission.
Payload Capacity:
The Gemini platform can accommodate payloads up to 20 kb, far surpassing the 4.18 kb limit of most current mRNA vaccines. This allows for more complex or multivalent vaccines, opening the door to combination therapies that require the expression of multiple antigens or larger therapeutic proteins.

Safety and logistics improvements: Our claims regarding the platform’s ability to remove the need for lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) are strongly supported by experimental data, which demonstrate enhanced safety, reduced toxicity, and simplified logistics compared to existing systems.

2. IgM plays a pivotal role in vaccine development, mainly due to its unique properties and early response in the immune system. As the first antibody produced during an immune response, IgM is essential for the initial defence against infections. In the context of vaccine development, this early response is critical for evaluating the efficacy of a vaccine candidate. Vaccines aim to mimic natural infection to elicit an immune response without causing disease, and the presence of IgM serves as an early indicator of the vaccine's ability to trigger an immune response. Moreover, IgM's pentameric structure allows it to effectively agglutinate pathogens, leading to enhanced pathogen clearance. This property is particularly important in vaccines targeting bacteria and viruses that rely on agglutination for effective neutralization. For instance, in the development of vaccines against encapsulated bacteria, such as Streptococcus pneumoniae, the IgM response can be a crucial measure of vaccine-induced immunity. Additionally, IgM has a high avidity for antigens, which is beneficial in the context of vaccines designed to elicit responses against highly variable pathogens, like influenza or HIV. In such cases, the ability of IgM to recognize a broad range of antigenic variants can provide an early line of defence against these rapidly mutating pathogens. Furthermore, the role of IgM in the maturation of the immune response is significant. The early IgM response can shape the subsequent IgG response, which is more specific and provides long-term immunity. Understanding how vaccines stimulate this transition from an IgM to an IgG response is essential in developing vaccines that provide lasting protection. In conclusion, IgM's role in the early immune response, its agglutinating ability, high avidity for antigens, and its influence on the maturation of the immune response make it a critical component in vaccine development. Its presence and functionality can significantly influence the design, testing, and evaluation of vaccines, particularly those targeting rapidly mutating or highly variable pathogens.

3. Immunogenicity Without LNP Encapsulation: We assessed whether LNP encapsulation was necessary for the immunogenicity of Gemini saRNA and saDNA vaccines by using eGFP as a model antigen. Our results demonstrated that Naked saDNA (50 µg) performed better (p = 0.0129) than 5 µg of LNP-encapsulated saDNA (p = 0.1983), while Naked saRNA (50 µg) also performed better (p = 0.0420) compared to its LNP-encapsulated counterpart (p = 0.3200) (Figure 10B-C). This suggests that LNP encapsulation may not be essential for eliciting a strong immune response. We further compared antibody responses among different vaccine formulations and found that Naked saDNA and Naked saRNA had comparable or better responses compared to LNP-encapsulated vaccines (Figure 10D-E). T cell responses measured by IFN-γ, IL-4, and TNF-α ELISPOT assays showed that Naked formats achieved similar or superior responses compared to LNP-encapsulated vaccines (Figures 10F-K). These findings indicate that Naked Gemini vaccines are highly effective and could potentially reduce formulation costs and complexity.
4. Durability of Antibody Responses: We conducted a time-course study to evaluate the durability of antibody responses elicited by Naked saDNA and saRNA vaccines expressing Omicron-Spike (Figure 12A). Our results showed that Naked saRNA vaccines provided durable responses up to 42 days, whereas Naked saDNA vaccines elicited durable responses lasting at least 70 days (Figure 12B). This extended durability of Naked saDNA responses suggests that it may be preferable for applications requiring long-term immune protection.
Viral Challenge and Vaccine Efficacy: To determine the efficacy of Naked saDNA compared to LNP-encapsulated saDNA, we performed viral challenge experiments. Mice were vaccinated with either Naked or LNP-encapsulated Omicron-Spike saDNA and challenged with SARS-CoV-2. We observed a significant reduction in viraemia in vaccinated mice compared to controls (Figure 13A-C). Notably, Naked saDNA vaccines demonstrated a marked reduction in nucleocapsid protein levels (p = 0.0003) and similar neutralization antibody levels to Naked saRNA vaccines (Figure 13C). This reduction in viraemia is crucial for developing effective vaccines that could potentially reduce severe respiratory outcomes associated with COVID-19.

Conventional mRNA Vaccine Impact: Conventional mRNA-based vaccines were critical in reducing the burden on healthcare systems and lowering mortality rates during the COVID-19 pandemic. However, despite their success, they faced significant technological challenges.
Technological Challenges in mRNA Vaccines: The main issues with mRNA vaccines included stability concerns, complex manufacturing processes, and the need for lipid nanoparticle (LNP) encapsulation. These challenges complicated vaccine production, distribution, and long-term storage, especially in resource-limited settings. Gemini Platform Overview: The Gemini platform represents a breakthrough in gene expression technology, utilizing both self-amplifying RNA (saRNA) and self-amplifying armed DNA (saDNA). This binary platform addresses many of the limitations faced by conventional mRNA vaccines. Stability and Storage: Unlike conventional mRNA vaccines, which degrade after one freeze-thaw cycle, the Gemini platform demonstrates exceptional stability through five freeze-thaw cycles. It can also be freeze-dried, stored, and distributed as a powder that can be reconstituted in aqueous solutions, providing significant long-term storage benefits. LNP Elimination and Manufacturing Simplification: A key strength of the Gemini platform is that both the saRNA and saDNA technologies bypass the need for LNP encapsulation, which is essential for mRNA vaccines like those from Moderna and Pfizer. This elimination of LNPs simplifies the manufacturing process, reduces associated costs, and mitigates potential toxicity and adverse reactions seen with LNPs. Cold Chain Management: Unlike mRNA vaccines, which require stringent refrigeration conditions (e.g., -20°C to -80°C), the Gemini platform formulations can be stored at ambient temperatures between 2°C and 8°C. This significantly improves cold chain management and reduces logistical challenges, particularly in remote or resource-limited settings. Extended Protein Expression: The Gemini platform offers prolonged protein expression for over 28 days, compared to the three days seen in conventional mRNA vaccines. This extended expression supports more robust and sustained immune responses, including both humoral antibodies and cell-mediated T lymphocytes. Payload Capacity: Another critical advantage of the Gemini platform is its ability to carry payloads of up to 16-20 kb, far exceeding the 4.18 kb limit of mRNA vaccines like those from Moderna and Pfizer. This larger payload allows for the expression of more complex or larger proteins, offering potential for multivalent vaccines and combined immunotherapies. Safety and Integration: The Gemini saRNA and saDNA platforms are several orders of magnitude safer than FDA standards for vector integration, reducing the risk of insertional mutagenesis. Viraemia Reduction: The naked self-amplifying armed DNA format of the Gemini platform has been shown to provide durable antibody responses and holds promise for curtailing viraemia, potentially reducing SARS-CoV-2 replication and transmission. Cost-Efficiency and Accessibility: Overall, the Gemini platform offers enhanced cost-efficiency and accessibility, making it a superior alternative not only for vaccines but also for the delivery of immunotherapeutics and other biologics. Broader Nanomedicine Applications: Beyond vaccines, the Gemini platform represents a significant advancement in nanomedicine, with applications in vaccine development, cancer treatment, and therapeutic protein delivery, demonstrating its versatility and broad potential.
